interpretation_notes: Treat the donor-matched pseudobulk model as paired only when the DE output confirms pseudobulk_design=paired.
For pseudobulk DE, pct.1 and pct.2 are fractions of pseudobulk samples with nonzero counts, not cell-level expression fractions.
Condition-only setdiff output is not a formal condition-by-cell-type interaction test.
Network prioritization scores are prioritization metrics, not p-values.
Cross-module agreement from the same dataset is convergence, not independent replication.
context.cell_state_reporting_instruction: When summarizing perturbation biology, use the quantitative group_state_summary from cell_state_analysis. If discussing lineage or cell-state composition, report the relevant state names together with their cell counts and percentages where available. Do not merely say that composition shifted. Distinguish this perturbation's state distribution from cross-target comparisons, and do not call a pathway a direct target-gene mechanism when the same signal could be explained by state-composition differences.

statistical_notes: Condition-only mode: setdiff; this is a set difference, not a formal condition-by-cell-type interaction test.
Adjusted p-values are corrected within each output table, not across the entire workflow.
PCA/UMAP are exploratory visualization outputs and should not be interpreted as formal statistical tests.
Enrichment depends on the submitted DE gene list and default service background unless a future custom background option is added.
Classifier feature selection is exploratory unless validation is sample-aware and feature selection is performed inside each training split.
Cell-level classifier splits can be optimistic if cells from the same biological sample are split across train/test; sample-level validation is preferred.
Pseudobulk DE aggregates raw counts by sample/replicate and group. Current pseudobulk method: limma_voom.
limma/voom pseudobulk uses edgeR filtering/TMM normalization, voom precision weights, and limma empirical Bayes moderation for replicate-level inference.

llm_claims: Type I interferon/JAK–STAT antiviral transcriptional program is induced within CD14+ monocytes after ~6 h IFN‑β and is the most plausible primary driver of the observed RNA changes.
NFκB/inflammatory signaling signatures are present but more consistent with a reactive or parallel response rather than the primary driver in IFN‑β–stimulated monocytes.
ER stress/UPR and apoptosis/DNA‑damage response signatures are detectable at low–moderate levels and are more consistent with stress‑reactive biology than with causation.

Enrichment for interferon‑β production/regulation terms may reflect induction of upstream regulators or feedback loops but does not by itself demonstrate endogenous IFN‑β production in monocytes under exogenous IFN‑β.
A modest Interferon‑γ signaling signature is detected but is likely due to gene‑set overlap with type I IFN responses rather than true IFN‑γ pathway activation in this assay.
Mild cell‑cycle/proliferation signals are likely artifacts/confounders in this acute immune‑stimulation context.

paper.title: Transcriptomic Characterization of Hypermutated Microsatellite Stable Tumors Reveals Distinct Proliferative and Immune Signatures
paper.abstract: Hypermutated microsatellite stable tumors are a subgroup of cancers, representing approximately 1-2% of colorectal tumors and frequently associated with loss of POLE function. These tumors show increased immunogenicity and biological features similar to microsatellite instability-high tumors. However, their transcriptomic characteristics remain poorly understood. Here, we provide the first transcriptomic and miRNA characterization of hypermutated microsatellite stable tumors across colorectal cancer and endometrial cancer using TCGA dataset. Hypermutated microsatellite stable tumors showed increased expression of immune-related genes including up-regulation of interferon-gamma signaling and chemokine-related pathways. Further, gene set enrichment analysis identified three pathways consistently up-regulated across cancer types: mTORC1 signaling, E2F targets, and G2M checkpoint, indicating increased proliferation and replication-associated activity. Protein-protein interaction networks supported the shared up-regulation of mTORC1, E2F, and G2M pathways and identified common groups of genes across tumor types, including WARS1, heat shock proteins (HSPA4, HSPA5, HSPA9), proteasome subunits (PSMA3, PSMA4), and SLC7A11. Analysis of precursor microRNA expression identified down-regulation of epithelial proliferation and nitric oxide-cGMP signaling pathways in hypermutated MSS tumors in both tumor types. Additionally, SLC7A11 was the only precursor microRNA-supported differentially expressed gene shared between colorectal and endometrial cancer. In colorectal cancer, SLC7A11 expression was associated with hsa-mir-9 family members, whereas in endometrial cancer it was linked to hsa-mir-92b. Previous studies have showed important role of SLC7A11 in oxidative-stress regulation and explored it as a potential therapeutic target in cancer Together, our results indicate that hypermutated MSS tumors share common immune and proliferation-associated pathways up-regulation across tumor types, while also showing cancer-specific regulatory and metabolic features. These findings provide additional evidence that hypermutated MSS tumors represent a biologically distinct subgroup with partial transcriptomic overlap with microsatellite instability-high tumors and may have potential clinical relevance.

paper.title: 2026 iCARDIO Alliance Global Implementation Guidelines on Heart Failure.
paper.abstract: This is the updated 2026 version of the iCARDIO Alliance Global Implementation Guidelines on Heart Failure - originally published in 2025. In these guidelines, we aim to consider inconsistencies in healthcare access, varying infrastructure, re-source constraints and diverse local practices as well as practical and political issues that restrict the global applicability of currently available guidelines. There is a need for universal recommendations that address the unique challenges faced by patients and healthcare providers worldwide. Our iCARDIO Alliance Global Implementation Guidelines emphasize the in-corporation of novel therapies, while integrating standard of care with the most up-to-date evidence to enable clinicians to optimize patient care. This document is about heart failure (HF), including acute and chronic heart failure, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction as well as HF with improved ejection frac-tion and cardiomyopathies. Context-specific recommendations tailored to individual patient needs are highlighted providing a thorough evaluation of the risks, benefits, and overall value of each therapy, aiming to establish a standard of care that im- proves patient outcomes and reduces the burden of hospitalization in this susceptible population. These guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations that represent a group consensus considering the many other published guide-lines that have reviewed many of the issues discussed here, but they also make new recommendations where new evidence has recently emerged. Most importantly these guidelines also provide recommendations on a number of issues where re-source limitations may put constraints on the care provided to HF patients. Such "economic adjustment" recommendations aim to provide guidance for situations when "Resources are somewhat limited" or when "Resources are severely limited". Hence, this document presents not only a comprehensive but also concise set of recommendations to guide all aspects of HF management with a unified strategy for the pharmacological, non-pharmacological, invasive and interventional man-agement of this significant global health challenge that is applicable to the needs of healthcare around the globe. paper.title: Mortality and disability after hospitalisation for injuries in low-income and middle-income countries: a cohort study.
paper.abstract:
Background

Mortality and disability after injuries are high in low-income and middle-income countries (LMICs). Improving outcomes for injured patients requires knowledge of their associated factors. We aimed to assess post-injury mortality and disability and their associations with access to health care across LMICs with different injury burdens, health-care systems, and contexts.

Methods

Hospitalised patients in Ghana, Pakistan, Rwanda, and South Africa with moderate-to-severe injuries were recruited and followed up until 3 months after discharge or death. Injured patients of any age who were admitted to facilities for more than 12 h or died within 12 h of admission were included. Data were collected between Feb 17, 2023, and Aug 31, 2024, using the REDCap electronic data platform. Our primary outcome was a composite of 3-month mortality or moderate-to-severe disability (assessed using the WHO Disability Assessment Schedule). Secondary outcomes were disability at 3 months after discharge, mortality up to 3 months after discharge (including in-hospital mortality), and in-hospital mortality. In multivariable analysis, we tested the associations of these outcomes with access to health-care variables of previous health-care encounters, transport to the hospital (private vs ambulance vs other), delays in reaching the hospital, and hospital level (secondary vs tertiary), controlling for age, sex, education, wealth, and injury type and severity.

Findings

9720 patients admitted to 19 hospitals capable of providing definitive care for injuries, serving urban and rural settings, were eligible for inclusion in the study. Of those, 8858 (91·1%; 6788 male, 2047 female, and 23 [<1%] with missing sex data; median age 31 years [IQR 20-43]) were enrolled and 8687 (89·4%) completed hospital follow-up, with 5835 patients followed up at 3 months. At 3 months, 2476 (47·6%) of 5199 patients with available primary outcome data had died or were disabled. In-hospital mortality was 6·1% (531 of 8687), 3-month mortality was 9·7% (616 of 6366), and 3-month disability was 40·6% (1860 of 4583). Higher odds of the primary outcome were associated with arrival by ambulance (odds ratio 1·86, 95% CI 1·51-2·29), and lower odds were associated with a previous health-care encounter (0·61, 0·52-0·71). Hospital level (1·14, 0·96-1·35) and delays in reaching the facility (0·86, 0·74-1·00) were not associated with the primary outcome.

Interpretation

The high post-injury mortality and disability are associated with health system factors that must be better understood before potentially expensive service models are introduced or expanded. Investment in pre-hospital care, ambulance systems, and centralised specialist trauma centres is unlikely to achieve its intended benefits unless services are appropriately planned, integrated, coordinated, and staffed across the care pathway. High-quality routine data are also essential to guide service improvement and enable robust quasi-experimental evaluations of whether these investments improve patient outcomes, for whom, and under what circumstances.

Funding

National Institute for Health and Care Research.

paper.title: Effects of a 3-day simulated heatwave on physiological and functional outcomes in older adults in Canada: a single-site randomised crossover trial.
paper.abstract:
Background

Laboratory-based heatwave simulations are a valuable tool for evaluating physiological and functional effects of heat exposure in vulnerable population groups (eg, older adults) and for testing the efficacy of personal cooling strategies. However, previous studies have been short in duration (2-9 h) and therefore have not captured the cumulative, multiday exposures characteristic of real-world heatwaves. We aimed to investigate physiological and functional outcomes in older adults exposed to a 3-day simulated heatwave.

Methods

We conducted a single-site, randomised, crossover trial at the Human and Environmental Physiology Research Unit at the University of Ottawa, ON, Canada. Participants were eligible if they lived in the Ottawa-Gatineau region, were aged 65-85 years, did not smoke, spoke English or French, and could provide informed consent. Exclusion criteria included severe physical restrictions, use of medication that made participation inadvisable, or cardiac abnormalities. Enrolled participants were exposed for 3 days (and 2 nights) to a simulated heatwave (34°C during the day and 26°C during the night with 45% relative humidity) and a thermoneutral control condition (26°C during both the day and night with 45% relative humidity) in a specialised climate chamber replicating a studio apartment. The two exposure sessions (ie, heatwave and control conditions) were separated by more than 10 days, and the order in which participants were assigned to each session was randomly allocated using a key generated in Microsoft Excel. Peak 1-h core (rectal) temperature was the primary outcome and was compared across days and conditions using linear mixed-effects models. Participants and investigators could not be masked to the exposure condition, but body temperature and heart rate data were processed by a masked analyst. All randomly assigned participants were included in the analyses; missing data were not imputed. The trial is registered with Clinicaltrials.gov (NCT06633302) and is complete.

Findings

Between Oct 15, 2024, and Feb 19, 2025, 22 individuals were screened and 18 eligible participants were enrolled; the median age of all participants was 74 years (IQR 71-78), nine (50%) of the 18 participants were female, and nine (50%) were male. All participants completed both intervention periods. Daily peak core temperature was 0·4°C (95% CI 0·3-0·4) higher during the simulated heatwave exposure than during the control exposure (cross-day average: 37·8°C [SD 0·2] vs 37·4°C [0·2]; p<0·0001). No adverse events occurred.

raw.abstractText:
Background

Laboratory-based heatwave simulations are a valuable tool for evaluating physiological and functional effects of heat exposure in vulnerable population groups (eg, older adults) and for testing the efficacy of personal cooling strategies. However, previous studies have been short in duration (2-9 h) and therefore have not captured the cumulative, multiday exposures characteristic of real-world heatwaves. We aimed to investigate physiological and functional outcomes in older adults exposed to a 3-day simulated heatwave.

Methods

We conducted a single-site, randomised, crossover trial at the Human and Environmental Physiology Research Unit at the University of Ottawa, ON, Canada. Participants were eligible if they lived in the Ottawa-Gatineau region, were aged 65-85 years, did not smoke, spoke English or French, and could provide informed consent. Exclusion criteria included severe physical restrictions, use of medication that made participation inadvisable, or cardiac abnormalities. Enrolled participants were exposed for 3 days (and 2 nights) to a simulated heatwave (34°C during the day and 26°C during the night with 45% relative humidity) and a thermoneutral control condition (26°C during both the day and night with 45% relative humidity) in a specialised climate chamber replicating a studio apartment. The two exposure sessions (ie, heatwave and control conditions) were separated by more than 10 days, and the order in which participants were assigned to each session was randomly allocated using a key generated in Microsoft Excel. Peak 1-h core (rectal) temperature was the primary outcome and was compared across days and conditions using linear mixed-effects models. Participants and investigators could not be masked to the exposure condition, but body temperature and heart rate data were processed by a masked analyst. All randomly assigned participants were included in the analyses; missing data were not imputed. The trial is registered with Clinicaltrials.gov (NCT06633302) and is complete.

Findings

Between Oct 15, 2024, and Feb 19, 2025, 22 individuals were screened and 18 eligible participants were enrolled; the median age of all participants was 74 years (IQR 71-78), nine (50%) of the 18 participants were female, and nine (50%) were male. All participants completed both intervention periods. Daily peak core temperature was 0·4°C (95% CI 0·3-0·4) higher during the simulated heatwave exposure than during the control exposure (cross-day average: 37·8°C [SD 0·2] vs 37·4°C [0·2]; p<0·0001). No adverse events occurred.

Interpretation

Older adults (aged 65-85 years) exposed to a simulated 3-day heatwave showed persistent daytime elevations in core temperature, highlighting the importance of evidence-based cooling strategies and other interventions to minimise physiological strain during even moderate heat stress, and not just during the most extreme conditions.

paper.title: To Whom National Culture Matters: An Analysis of Mentions of Countries in Titles and Abstracts in Social and Personality Psychology and Related Fields From 1990 to 2020.
paper.abstract: Culture significantly influences human psychology, making it essential for psychological research, particularly in social psychology, to acknowledge its importance. However, the majority of psychological research ignores or marginalises culture and context. This is problematic because, despite representing a small portion of humanity (specifically Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich and Democratic (WEIRD) populations) mainstream psychology is published as if it represented the whole humanity. Among the subfields of psychology, social psychology is arguably the one in which this issue should be least prevalent. To investigate this, we conducted a study on titles and abstracts of articles from 69 social psychology journals published between 1990 and 2020, examining how cultural diversity and awareness of its importance changed over time. The results indicate that cultural awareness is more prominent in journals focused on culture, international or local issues; while remaining almost entirely absent in journals focused on theory, reviews and business. Furthermore, cultural awareness displays an imbalance regarding culture: while WEIRD mentions remain most common, mentions of other regions appear to be disproportionately represented or 'inflated' in specific contexts. The generalizability of psychological theories will remain impossible if culture is not integrated as a central factor in research.

paper.title: ICAM signaling rewires the inflammatory communication network in pediatric gout.
paper.abstract:
Introduction

The immune regulatory characteristics and core inflammatory signaling networks of pediatric gout have not been fully elucidated. The prevailing view of generalized immune hyperactivation cannot precisely explain the unique immune pathological features of pediatric gout, highlighting an urgent research gap to be addressed.

Methods

To clarify the immune regulatory mechanism of pediatric gout, we performed single-cell transcriptomic profiling and systematic cell-cell interaction analysis on peripheral blood samples collected from pediatric gout patients and healthy controls. We comprehensively compared the intercellular communication networks, signaling pathway activities, and molecular expression patterns between the two groups, and focused on the differential inflammatory signaling axes dominating pediatric gout pathogenesis.

Results

Different from the traditional view of global immune hyperactivation, pediatric gout exhibited a highly selective remodeling of circulating immune networks. The ICAM signaling pathway was identified as the most dominant and disease-specific inflammatory axis in pediatric gout. In the immune communication network, platelets served as the major signal-emitting hubs with significantly enhanced signaling activity in patients, while CD14+ monocytes acted as the primary signal recipients. Selective upregulation of ICAM1 was detected in CD14+ monocytes of pediatric gout patients, which endowed monocytes with strengthened signal -receiving capacity. Notably, other classic immune pathways showed no significant differences between patients and healthy controls.

Discussion

This study demonstrates that pediatric gout is characterized by directional and selective immune crosstalk rather than universal immune activation. The ICAM-centered inflammatory interactome is the core driver of immune network remodeling in pediatric gout. These findings complement and advance previous single-cell research on adult gout, and identify the ICAM signaling pathway as a novel and promising therapeutic target for the precise clinical intervention of pediatric gout.
